   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?

   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?

   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?

   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?

   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?

   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?

Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: AstraZeneca is a top dog in fast-growing niches such as antibody-drug conjugates (Enhertu) and EGFR lung cancer, with a visionary long-serving CEO and a $80B 2030 revenue ambition, but it is a large, established pharma company growing revenue around 8-9% a year, not the leader of a new, emerging industry. The shares are down from about $208 in February 2026 to $165, so it also lacks Gardner's momentum trait.
summaries.buffett: AstraZeneca has durable patent-protected franchises, an 83% core gross margin in H1 2026 and has turned FY2025 net profit of $10,225M into about $8,670M of free cash flow after all capital spending, but its products must be constantly replaced as patents expire and net debt was $26,912M at June 30, 2026. At about 25 times trailing reported earnings and 5 times book value, a Buffett-style buyer would see a good business without a clear margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would respect the rationality of a science-led company that turned a weak pipeline into 43 approvals in a year, but inverting shows clear failure paths: US generics of Farxiga in 2026, US price controls, China investigations and costly trial failures. It looks like a good business at a full-to-fair price rather than an obvious bargain.
summaries.lynch: AstraZeneca is a classic stalwart: large, dividend-paying, with Total Revenue up from $26,617M in FY2020 to $58,739M in FY2025 and consensus about 8% growth for 2026. At about 16 times forward core EPS against roughly 11% core EPS growth (and about 25 times trailing reported EPS), the PEG is above 1, so Lynch's price test is not met.
summaries.fisher: AstraZeneca scores very well on Fisher's research and sales points: $14,232M of R&D in FY2025, more than 100 Phase 3 trials, 43 approvals in major regions in the year to February 2026 and strong launch execution in oncology and China. Weaker points are the reliance on acquisitions and licensing (Alexion, CSPC) and a 2024 China investigation that clouds governance.
summaries.graham: AstraZeneca passes Graham's size, ten-year profitability and long dividend-record tests, but fails the price tests badly: about 33 times three-year average reported EPS and about 5 times book value, far above the 15x and 22.5 limits, and its current ratio was below 1 at June 30, 2026. A defensive Graham investor would not buy at today's price.
summaries.thiel: AstraZeneca holds temporary monopolies through patents on drugs such as Tagrisso, Enhertu and Ultomiris and has a powerful global distribution engine, but none rests on a 10x technology or a secret others cannot see, and each monopoly expires. Durability depends on the pipeline continually replacing products that lose exclusivity.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable growth at a reasonable price; AstraZeneca offers high-single-digit revenue growth, low-double-digit core EPS growth and a 34% core operating margin at about 16 times forward core earnings. It is a reasonable quality-at-fair-price holding, though not exposed to the AI platform shift he emphasises.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller-style analysis would note rising earnings (H1 2026 core EPS +12% and a Q2 core EPS beat) and catalysts such as the Baxfendy launch and obesity data, but the share price has trended down since February 2026 and Farxiga generics weigh on growth. There is no strong liquidity or momentum tailwind to justify a concentrated bet.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith would like the 82-83% gross margin, consistent revenue growth since 2020 and broad diversification, but would note that reported returns on capital are diluted by $21,181M of goodwill and $37,723M of intangibles and that cash conversion is weaker than at the best consumer or software franchises. At about 25 times trailing reported earnings it is good but not cheap.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula AstraZeneca screens poorly: FY2025 operating profit of $13,743M is only about 4.8% of its roughly $283B enterprise value, and returns on tangible capital are hard to read given heavy acquired intangibles. It would not rank among the cheapest high-return stocks.
summaries.akre: AstraZeneca partly fits Akre's three-legged stool: a strong, patent-protected business, a capable long-serving CEO in Pascal Soriot, and ample reinvestment opportunities in R&D. The weak leg is compounding per share, since the share count rose from 1,313M (FY2020) to 1,562M (FY2025) with the Alexion deal and dividends absorb about half of profit.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho approach seeks simple businesses in temporary distress at a deep discount; AstraZeneca is a complex pharma company at a full valuation, with downside limited by diversification but no obvious mispricing. The chance of permanent loss is low, but the heads-I-win, tails-I-don't-lose-much asymmetry is not evident.
summaries.wood: AstraZeneca is not a pure-play disruptive innovator in ARK's sense, though it combines several innovation platforms such as antibody-drug conjugates, cell therapy, radioconjugates and genomics-driven drug discovery. Its addressable market grows steadily rather than many-fold, so it fits ARK's framework only loosely.
summaries.ackman: Ackman looks for simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and strong balance sheets; AstraZeneca generates strong cash and holds dominant niche positions, but drug pipelines are hard to predict and net debt is about 1.8 times FY2025 operating cash flow. It partly fits, without an obvious activist angle.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's scale-economies-shared model (passing scale savings to customers) does not describe a pharma company that relies on patent pricing; AstraZeneca's scale funds R&D rather than lowering prices. Its long-term position may stay strong but is not clearly getting stronger in the self-reinforcing way Sleep sought.
summaries.valentine: AstraZeneca's medicines solve large, painful problems such as cancer, heart and kidney disease and rare disorders, which fits Valentine's emphasis on big markets with real pain. But it is a mature incumbent rather than a young company riding a new technology wave, so most of his venture-oriented questions do not apply strongly.
summaries.nash: AstraZeneca passes Nash's checks for profitability, a clear story and size, but fails several hard filters: gross debt of $32,239M exceeds cash of $4,968M, revenue growth is below 10% and its operating margin of 23.4% (FY2025 reported) is just under 25%. Its Nash scorecard total is about 70 and a 12% DCF value is well below the $165 share price, so it does not qualify as a Nash buy.

momentum.evidence: The NYSE share price fell from about $208 in February 2026 to $165.41 on October 16, 2026, roughly flat versus a split-adjusted $162 a year earlier, lagging a rising market.

g4.evidence: Pascal Soriot has led the company since 2012, and it partners with leading firms such as Daiichi Sankyo (Enhertu, Datroway) and Amgen (Tezspire).

g6.evidence: Analysts are mostly positive: 10 of 12 rate it Buy or Strong Buy with an average price target of $207.16, about 25% above the October 16, 2026 price.

simple.evidence: The business model (patented medicines sold to health systems) is clear, but judging a pipeline of more than 100 Phase 3 trials and patent cliffs requires specialist knowledge.

b2.evidence: Total Revenue rose every year from $26,617M in FY2020 to $58,739M in FY2025, and the company has been profitable every year in that period.

integrity.evidence: Reporting is detailed and the company reconfirmed guidance in July 2026, but CEO pay is among the highest in the FTSE 100 and its China president was detained in 2024 amid local investigations.

b6.evidence: Most growth is organic R&D, but it has made large deals such as the 2021 Alexion acquisition and a $1,104M upfront payment to CSPC in H1 2026.

roic.evidence: Return on equity was about 20% in FY2025 ($10,225M profit on about $50B of equity), helped by net debt of $26,912M, and returns on total capital are diluted by $21,181M of goodwill.

fcf.evidence: FY2025 operating cash flow of $14,575M less $2,810M of property and $3,095M of intangible purchases left about $8,670M, about 85% of the $10,225M net profit.

b10.evidence: Retained profit and the Alexion deal more than doubled revenue from $26,617M (FY2020) to $58,739M (FY2025), but diluted shares rose from 1,313M to 1,562M over the same period.

safety.evidence: A conservative DCF (8-10% growth, 15-20% FCF margin, 12% discount rate) gives roughly $70-110 per share, below the $165.41 price.

fairprice.evidence: About 16 times FY2026 consensus core EPS of $10.22 for roughly 11% core EPS growth is reasonable for a diversified pharma leader, but about 25 times trailing reported EPS is not cheap.

mu5.evidence: A broad portfolio across oncology, CVRM, rare disease and respiratory limits single-product risk, but patent expiries, US price controls and China investigations are real failure paths.

reinvest.evidence: It reinvests heavily ($14,232M R&D in FY2025) with high productivity (43 approvals in the year to February 2026) and says it is on track for $80B of revenue in 2030.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart: a large, dividend-paying company growing revenue about 8% a year with a simple story of new medicines replacing ageing ones.

ly3.evidence: Forward P/E of about 16 on core EPS growth of about 11.5% (and trailing reported P/E of about 25) is above the earnings growth rate.

runway.evidence: Growth drivers include Enhertu, Imfinzi, Baxfendy (US approval May 2026) and obesity candidate elecoglipron, supporting the $80B 2030 revenue ambition.

ly7.evidence: The share count is flat (diluted 1,562M in FY2023 and FY2025, 1,560M in Q2 2026), there is no buyback, and no notable open-market insider buying was found.

ly8.evidence: It is one of the largest UK companies, widely covered (25 analysts in FY2026 revenue consensus), and not a boring overlooked niche.

fi2.evidence: It keeps launching new medicines as older ones mature, such as Baxfendy in 2026 as Farxiga lost US exclusivity, backed by more than 100 Phase 3 trials.

fi3.evidence: R&D of $14,232M in FY2025 produced 43 approvals in major regions in the year to February 2026 and blockbusters such as Tagrisso, Imfinzi and Enhertu.

fi4.evidence: Strong commercial execution built leading positions in oncology and in China ($6,654M of FY2025 revenue), with launches such as Enhertu growing 36% in H1 2026.

longterm.evidence: Management has raised R&D spending to $14,232M and committed $50 billion to US manufacturing and R&D over five years, prioritising long-term pipeline growth.

gr1.evidence: FY2025 Total Revenue was $58,739M and its market value is about $256B.

ni10.evidence: It has been profitable every year in the last decade, with the low point a $112M profit attributable to shareholders in 2021 after Alexion acquisition charges.

gr4.evidence: AstraZeneca has paid dividends every year since its 1999 formation and intends to raise the FY2026 dividend to $3.30 per share.

eps10.evidence: Reported basic EPS rose from about $1.03 in 2019 ($1,335M on 1,301M shares) to $6.60 in FY2025, well over a one-third increase.

gr6.evidence: The price of $165.41 is about 33 times average reported EPS of $4.99 over FY2023-FY2025.

gr7.evidence: Trailing P/E of about 25 times price to book of about 5.1 (market value about $256B vs $50,295M equity at June 30, 2026) gives about 126, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Some drugs are clearly superior in their niches, such as Enhertu in HER2 breast cancer, but none is ten times better than the next best alternative.

timing.evidence: Ageing populations, the ADC wave and demand for obesity and hypertension drugs make the timing favourable for its pipeline.

th3.evidence: It is already a large company, but franchises such as Tagrisso began in a narrow EGFR-mutated lung cancer niche and expanded into earlier-stage disease.

team.evidence: Pascal Soriot, CEO since 2012 and knighted in 2022, led the turnaround that more than doubled revenue from FY2020 to FY2025.

th5.evidence: It sells in more than 100 countries with a strong salesforce and a leading position in China.

durable.evidence: Its scale, R&D engine and diversified portfolio should endure, but each product's position lasts only until patent expiry, as Farxiga showed in 2026.

th7.evidence: Its early bets on China and on ADCs with Daiichi Sankyo were insights rivals were slow to copy, but they are no longer unique.

trend.evidence: It benefits from ageing populations and the shift to targeted cancer therapies like ADCs, but not from AI or cloud computing as a core business.

dr1.evidence: H1 2026 core EPS rose 12% and Q2 core EPS of $2.63 beat consensus, but revenue growth is steady at 6% CER rather than accelerating.

dr2.evidence: Baxfendy, Enhertu and obesity data could improve the picture, but the Farxiga generic decline and US pricing reforms are offsets the market already sees.

dr4.evidence: Pharma demand is largely independent of the economy, but net debt of $26,912M makes it modestly sensitive to interest rates.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include the Q3 2026 results, the US Baxfendy launch, Phase III progress for elecoglipron and readouts for Datroway and other late-stage drugs.

dr7.evidence: It is a high-quality diversified holding, but patent cliffs and pricing risks argue against a very concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Core gross margin was 83% in H1 2026, a sign of strong pricing power on patented drugs.

fcfyield.evidence: FCF of about $8,670M (after all capital spending) to $11,765M (after property only) in FY2025 is a 3.4-4.6% yield on a $256B market value, moderate for its growth.

gb2.evidence: FY2025 operating profit of $13,743M is about 4.8% of an enterprise value of about $283B.

pa2.evidence: US Farxiga generics and pricing pressure are real but manageable headwinds rather than a deep, temporary crisis.

pa4.evidence: With FY2025 revenue of $58,739M across many drugs and positive cash flow, permanent capital loss seems unlikely at today's valuation.

wo1.evidence: It is not a leader in ARK's listed platforms, though it uses genomics and AI within its drug research.

wo2.evidence: Drug production costs do not fall in a way that unlocks large new demand; pricing is set by patents and payers.

wo3.evidence: It combines ADCs, cell therapy, radioconjugates and genomics-driven discovery, but these serve one industry rather than converging technology platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its 2030 ambition of $80B is about 1.4 times FY2025 revenue of $58,739M, not many times larger.

ac3.evidence: Medicine demand is largely insulated from commodities and the economy, though currency movements affect reported results.

ns1.evidence: It does not pass scale savings to customers through lower prices; its model relies on patent-protected pricing.

ns4.evidence: A stronger pipeline and the $80B 2030 ambition point upward, but patent expiries on Tagrisso, Lynparza and Soliris make a clearly stronger position uncertain.

va2.evidence: Its medicines treat cancer, heart and kidney disease, asthma and rare disorders, which are large and painful problems.

tn1.evidence: It rides the ageing and targeted-oncology trends but is a traditional pharma company, not a business built for AI, energy or robotics.

tn2.evidence: The market sees a steady big pharma, while it is building positions in obesity, hypertension and cell therapy, but the gap is modest.

tn3.evidence: It is a UK-based large-cap pharma company, outside the avoided zones, although China is a material market.

tn4.evidence: It passes two of three: revenue grew every year from FY2020 to FY2025 and it is profitable, but gross debt of $32,239M exceeds cash of $4,968M.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow has been positive, but debt has exceeded cash in every recent quarter (net debt $26,912M at June 30, 2026).

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 8.6% in FY2025 and 9% (6% CER) in H1 2026, below 10%.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of 8.6% plus an FCF margin of about 15-20% gives about 23-29, below 40.

tn8.evidence: In FY2025 revenue grew 8.6% while total operating costs (revenue minus operating profit) rose about 2%, from $44,070M to $44,996M.

tn9.evidence: It trips the more-debt-than-cash kill ($32,239M gross debt vs $4,968M cash) and its FY2025 reported operating margin of 23.4% is close to the 20% line.

tn10.evidence: It faces US Medicare price negotiation, the October 2025 TrumpRx pricing agreement and investigations in China.

tn11.evidence: It provides patented medicines that help patients with cancer, heart, kidney, lung and rare diseases live longer, and charges health systems and insurers per prescription.

tn13.evidence: Total about 70: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin 5, short interest 10, institutional ownership 10, revenue vs expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 0, moat 5, CEO 10, pricing power 5, secular trend 5, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year from FY2020 to FY2025, but debt exceeded cash every year and the operating margin fell in FY2021 before recovering.

tn18.evidence: Soriot has 14 years in the role and a strong execution record, but he is not a founder and no significant open-market share purchases were found.

tn20.evidence: Q2 2026 core EPS of $2.63 beat consensus of about $2.50, but revenue was roughly in line and a longer record was not verified.

tn21.evidence: Margins are rising and there is no accounting concern, but the 2024 detention of its China president and frequent licensing and acquisition deals are yellow flags.

tn22.evidence: It has $58,739M of revenue, $10,225M of FY2025 profit and no share issuance to raise cash.
